claims.text: Adding approximately 3 at.% Al to a MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy will promote formation of Al-rich nanoprecipitates.
The Al-rich nanoprecipitates will be coherent with the refractory-alloy matrix.
The Al-rich nanoprecipitates will hinder dislocation motion at elevated temperature.
The Al addition will improve high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
The Al addition will lower alloy density.
The Al addition will preserve room-temperature mechanical performance.
Conventional melting and thermomechanical treatment can produce a homogeneous baseline MoNbTaW or similar refractory HEA microstructure.
The low density of Al will produce an overall reduction in alloy density when approximately 3 at.% Al is added.
The nanoprecipitates will strengthen the alloy primarily through precipitation hardening, including Orowan looping.
Precipitation hardening will impede high-temperature dislocation glide and reduce creep rates.
The proposed precipitation-hardening mechanism will not substantially alter room-temperature dislocation dynamics.
The Al-doped alloy will have approximately 15–20% or greater high-temperature yield-strength improvement relative to the Al-free baseline.
The Al-doped alloy will have an approximately 5% lower density than the Al-free baseline.
The Al-doped alloy will retain room-temperature strength and ductility comparable to the baseline.
The expected high-temperature improvement should occur at approximately 1000–1300°C under sustained loading.
The proposed benefit depends on formation of the desired precipitate morphology without detrimental embrittlement.
Precipitate coarsening could cause adverse room-temperature embrittlement.
